claim: The BBSome mediates dynamic trafficking of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) out of cilia.
source: Dynamic trafficking of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) out of cilia is mediated by the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of the BBSome.

claim: The BBSome, in concert with ARL6/BBS3, ferries GPCRs across the transition zone.
source: In concert with its membrane recruitment factor, the small GTPase ARL6/BBS3, the BBSome ferries GPCRs across the transition zone, a diffusion barrier at the base of cilia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the mechanism of BBSome function.

claim: The transition zone is a diffusion barrier at the base of cilia.
source: In concert with its membrane recruitment factor, the small GTPase ARL6/BBS3, the BBSome ferries GPCRs across the transition zone, a diffusion barrier at the base of cilia.
evidence: This is stated as a defining characteristic of the transition zone.

claim: Near-atomic structures of the BBSome by itself and in complex with ARL6GTP were determined.
source: Here, we present the near-atomic structures of the BBSome by itself and in complex with ARL6GTP, and we describe the changes in BBSome conformation induced by ARL6GTP binding.
evidence: This is the primary experimental result reported in the abstract.

claim: ARL6GTP binding induces conformational changes in the BBSome.
source: Here, we present the near-atomic structures of the BBSome by itself and in complex with ARL6GTP, and we describe the changes in BBSome conformation induced by ARL6GTP binding.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the structural studies.

claim: SMO and likely other GPCR cargoes must release their amphipathic helix 8 from the membrane to be recognized by the BBSome.
source: Modeling the interactions of the BBSome with membranes and the GPCR Smoothened (SMO) reveals that SMO, and likely also other GPCR cargoes, must release their amphipathic helix 8 from the membrane to be recognized by the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from modeling studies.

claim: Cilia dynamically concentrate signaling receptors to sense and transduce signals.
source: Cilia dynamically concentrate signaling receptors to sense and transduce signals as varied as light, odorant molecules, Hedgehog morphogens and ligands of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) (Anvarian et al., 2019; Bangs and Anderson, 2017; Nachury and Mick, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Hedgehog signal transduction relies on the disappearance of GPR161 and Patched 1 from cilia and the accumulation of SMO within cilia.
source: Highlighting the functional importance of dynamic ciliary trafficking, the appropriate transduction of Hedgehog signal relies on the disappearance of the GPCR GPR161 and the Hedgehog receptor Patched 1 from cilia and the accumulation of the GPCR Smoothened (SMO) within cilia (Bangs and Anderson, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Regulated exit from cilia represents a general mechanism to redistribute signaling molecules on demand.
source: Regulated exit from cilia represents a general mechanism to redistribute signaling molecules on demand (Nachury and Mick, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a general principle with a supporting citation.

claim: The BBSome is an evolutionarily conserved complex of eight Bardet-Biedl Syndrome (BBS) proteins.
source: Patched 1, GPR161, SMO and other ciliary membrane proteins are all ferried out of cilia in a regulated manner by an evolutionarily conserved complex of eight Bardet-Biedl Syndrome (BBS) proteins, the BBSome (Nachury, 2018; Wingfield et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: GPR161 and SSTR3 are removed from cilia by the BBSome only when they become activated.
source: While GPR161 and other ciliary GPCRs such as the Somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3) are removed from cilia by the BBSome only when they become activated, SMO undergoes constitutive BBSome-dependent exit from cilia in unstimulated cells to keep its ciliary levels low.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference in how different GPCRs are regulated by the BBSome.

claim: SMO undergoes constitutive BBSome-dependent exit from cilia in unstimulated cells to keep its ciliary levels low.
source: While GPR161 and other ciliary GPCRs such as the Somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3) are removed from cilia by the BBSome only when they become activated, SMO undergoes constitutive BBSome-dependent exit from cilia in unstimulated cells to keep its ciliary levels low.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of SMO regulation.

claim: Accumulation of SMO in cilia is achieved by suppression of its exit.
source: Accumulation of SMO in cilia is then, at least in part, achieved by suppression of its exit (Milenkovic et al., 2015; Nachury and Mick, 2019; Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism with supporting citations.

claim: Membrane proteins travel into, out of, and within cilia without utilizing vesicular intermediates and remain within the plane of the ciliary membrane.
source: Membrane proteins travel into, out of, and within cilia without utilizing vesicular intermediates and remain within the plane of the ciliary membrane (Breslow et al., 2013; Chadha et al., 2019; Milenkovic et al., 2009; Ye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Membrane proteins that enter and exit cilia must cross the transition zone by lateral transport.
source: Thus, membrane proteins that enter and exit cilia must cross the transition zone (TZ), a diffusion barrier at the base of cilia, by lateral transport (Garcia-Gonzalo and Reiter, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence with a supporting citation.

claim: Regulated TZ crossing of GPR161 is enabled by the BBSome in concert with ARL6/BBS3.
source: Recently, we found that regulated TZ crossing of GPR161 is enabled by the BBSome in concert with the ARF-like GTPase ARL6/BBS3 (Ye et al., 2018), but the mechanism of facilitated TZ crossing by the BBSome remains a fundamental unanswered question (Nachury and Mick, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with a supporting citation.

claim: The BBSome exists mostly in an auto-inhibited, closed conformation in solution.
source: Our recent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the BBSome revealed that the BBSome exists mostly in an auto-inhibited, closed conformation in solution and undergoes a conformational change as it is recruited to membranes by ARL6GTP (Chou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous cryo-EM study with a supporting citation.

claim: The BBSome undergoes a conformational change as it is recruited to membranes by ARL6GTP.
source: Our recent cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the BBSome revealed that the BBSome exists mostly in an auto-inhibited, closed conformation in solution and undergoes a conformational change as it is recruited to membranes by ARL6GTP (Chou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous cryo-EM study with a supporting citation.

claim: ARL6GTP triggers polymerization of a membrane-apposed BBSome/ARL6 coat.
source: Given that ARL6GTP triggers polymerization of a membrane-apposed BBSome/ARL6 coat (Jin et al., 2010) and enables BBSome-mediated TZ crossing (Ye et al., 2018), the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome conformation represents the active form of the complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: ARL6GTP enables BBSome-mediated TZ crossing.
source: Given that ARL6GTP triggers polymerization of a membrane-apposed BBSome/ARL6 coat (Jin et al., 2010) and enables BBSome-mediated TZ crossing (Ye et al., 2018), the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome conformation represents the active form of the complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The ARL6GTP-bound BBSome conformation represents the active form of the complex.
source: Given that ARL6GTP triggers polymerization of a membrane-apposed BBSome/ARL6 coat (Jin et al., 2010) and enables BBSome-mediated TZ crossing (Ye et al., 2018), the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome conformation represents the active form of the complex.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on cited evidence.

claim: SMO must eject its amphipathic helix 8 (SMOH8) from the inner leaflet of the membrane in order to be recognized by the BBSome.
source: Surprisingly, our studies reveal that SMO must eject its amphipathic helix 8 (SMOH8) from the inner leaflet of the membrane in order to be recognized by the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a surprising finding from the current studies.

claim: Ejection of amphipathic helix 8 from the membrane may be a general principle for the interaction of the BBSome with its cargo GPCRs.
source: Sequence analysis suggests that this may be a general principle for the interaction of the BBSome with its cargo GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on sequence analysis.

claim: The BBSome was purified to near-homogeneity from retinal extract.
source: Following on our previous strategy (Chou et al., 2019), we purified the BBSome to near-homogeneity from retinal extract and analyzed its structure by single-particle cryo-EM.
evidence: This is stated as a method used in the study.

claim: A BBSome map at an overall resolution of 3.4 Å was obtained from an initial dataset of 770,345 particles.
source: The advent of higher throughput direct detector cameras and faster automated data-collection procedures combined with improvements in data processing with new tools implemented in RELION-3 (Zivanov et al., 2018) led to a BBSome map at an overall resolution of 3.4 Å from an initial dataset of 770,345 particles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to supporting figures.

claim: The BBSome is composed of 29 distinct domains characteristic of sorting complexes.
source: The BBSome is composed of 29 distinct domains characteristic of sorting complexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic with reference to a figure.

claim: α-solenoids, β-propellers, pleckstrin homology (PH) and appendage domains are all present in multiple copies in the BBSome.
source: α-solenoids, β-propellers, pleckstrin homology (PH) and appendage domains are all present in multiple copies and our previous map made it possible to build a Cα backbone model that encompassed 25 out of 29 domains (PDB-Dev accession PDBDEV_00000018; Chou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic with reference to a previous study.

claim: A previous Cα backbone model encompassed 25 out of 29 domains.
source: α-solenoids, β-propellers, pleckstrin homology (PH) and appendage domains are all present in multiple copies and our previous map made it possible to build a Cα backbone model that encompassed 25 out of 29 domains (PDB-Dev accession PDBDEV_00000018; Chou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a result from a previous study with a citation.

claim: The higher-resolution map enabled confident assignment of side chains for most regions.
source: For building the current model, the previous Cα model was docked into the map, and the higher-resolution map enabled us to confidently assign side chains for most regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an improvement enabled by the new map.

claim: The new map allowed building of the coiled-coil domains of BBS1 and BBS9.
source: The new map allowed us to build the coiled-coil domains of BBS1 and BBS9, for which densities were not well-defined in the previous map.
evidence: This is stated as an improvement over the previous map.

claim: 27 out of 29 domains distributed across the 8 BBSome subunits could be modeled.
source: Altogether, 27 out of 29 domains distributed across the 8 BBSome subunits could be modeled.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the modeling effort.

claim: The gamma-adaptin ear (GAE) domains of BBS2 and BBS7 could not be modeled despite the increased resolution.
source: Despite the increased resolution of the current density map, the gamma-adaptin ear (GAE) domains of BBS2 and BBS7 could not be modeled, and side chains could not be assigned for BBS2βprop, BBS2cc, BBS7βprop and BBS7cc.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current map.

claim: Side chains could not be assigned for BBS2βprop, BBS2cc, BBS7βprop and BBS7cc.
source: Despite the increased resolution of the current density map, the gamma-adaptin ear (GAE) domains of BBS2 and BBS7 could not be modeled, and side chains could not be assigned for BBS2βprop, BBS2cc, BBS7βprop and BBS7cc.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current map.

claim: The new BBSome structure cannot accommodate binding to ARL6GTP.
source: Consistent with our previous observations based on a 4.9 Å resolution map of the BBSome (Chou et al., 2019), the new BBSome structure cannot accommodate binding to ARL6GTP.
evidence: This is stated as a finding consistent with previous observations.

claim: Fitting a homology model of the bovine BBS1βprop–ARL6GTP complex in the BBSome structure caused a steric clash between ARL6GTP and a region encompassing BBS2βprop and BBS7cc.
source: Fitting a homology model of the bovine BBS1βprop–ARL6GTP complex (based on the X-ray structure of the Chlamydomonas complex; Mourão et al., 2014) in either BBSome structure caused a steric clash between ARL6GTP and a region encompassing BBS2βprop and BBS7cc.
evidence: This is stated as a result from modeling with a citation.

claim: The BBSome exists in an autoinhibited form in solution and undergoes a conformational opening upon recruitment to membranes by ARL6GTP.
source: These data support a model in which the BBSome exists in an autoinhibited form in solution and undergoes a conformational opening upon recruitment to membranes by ARL6GTP, similar to other sorting complexes such as COPI, AP-1 and AP-2 (Cherfils, 2014; Faini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by the data and similar to other sorting complexes.

claim: Mixing recombinant ARL6GTP together with the purified BBSome allowed for complex formation in solution.
source: Mixing recombinant ARL6GTP together with the purified BBSome allowed for complex formation in solution.
evidence: This is stated as a method used in the study.

claim: The BBSome–ARL6GTP complex was analyzed by cryo-EM, yielding a density map at an overall resolution of 4.0 Å.
source: The BBSome–ARL6GTP complex was analyzed by cryo-EM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), yielding a density map at an overall resolution of 4.0 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to supporting figures.

claim: Focused refinement of the top and lower lobes of the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex resulted in improved maps of 3.8 Å and 4.2 Å resolution.
source: Focused refinement of the top and lower lobes of the complex resulted in improved maps of 3.8 Å and 4.2 Å resolution, which facilitated model building (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to a supporting figure.

claim: Several domains were better resolved in the density map of the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex compared to the BBSome alone.
source: Even though the apparent overall resolution was nominally not as good as that of the BBSome alone, several domains were better resolved in the density map of the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to a supporting figure.

claim: The quality of the map was significantly increased for the top β-propeller in the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex.
source: In particular, the quality of the map was significantly increased for the top β-propeller (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to a supporting figure.

claim: The improved map quality allowed correct placement of the β-propellers (βprop) of BBS2 and BBS7, which had been swapped in the previous structural description.
source: The improved map quality allowed us to correctly place the β-propellers (βprop) of BBS2 and BBS7, which had been swapped in our previous structural description (Chou et al., 2019) due to their extreme similarity and the limited resolution of the previous map.
evidence: This is stated as a correction to a previous error with a citation.

claim: The new assignment of BBS2 and BBS7 β-propellers is supported by a recently published structure of the BBSome.
source: This new assignment is further supported by a recently published structure of the BBSome (Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as additional support with a citation.

claim: In the BBSome–ARL6 structure, ARL6GTP is nestled in a wedge opening between BBS1βprop and BBS7βprop.
source: In the BBSome–ARL6 structure, ARL6GTP is nestled in a wedge opening between BBS1βprop and BBS7βprop.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: A ~ 20° rotation of BBS1βprop from the BBSome alone conformation allows ARL6GTP to move away from the steric clash with BBS2βprop.
source: A ~ 20° rotation of BBS1βprop from the BBSome alone conformation allows ARL6GTP to move away from the steric clash with BBS2βprop.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: The movement of BBS1βprop is accompanied by a twisting of the first two TPR repeats from the BBS4 α-solenoid.
source: This movement of BBS1βprop is accompanied by a twisting of the first two TPR repeats from the BBS4 α-solenoid (Video 1), in line with the close association between the N terminus of BBS4 and BBS1βprop seen in the BBSome alone structure and confirmed by cross-link mass spectrometry (Chou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a video and citation.

claim: Besides the movements of BBS1βprop and BBS4TPR1-2, ARL6GTP binding caused only subtle changes in the structure of the BBSome.
source: Besides the movements of BBS1βprop and BBS4TPR1-2, ARL6GTP binding caused only subtle changes in the structure of the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: The movements of BBS4 and BBS1 are in agreement with two recently published structures of the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome.
source: The movements of BBS4 and BBS1 are in agreement with two recently published structures of the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome (Klink et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as agreement with other published structures with citations.

claim: The conformational opening of the BBSome is likely spontaneous as a minor 3D class corresponding to the open form could be detected in the previous dataset of the BBSome alone.
source: We note that the conformational opening of the BBSome is likely spontaneous as a minor 3D class corresponding to the open form could be detected in our previous dataset of the BBSome alone.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from data analysis.

claim: The equilibrium between closed and open form in solution is strongly shifted towards the closed form.
source: As the 3D class of the open conformation contained only a small percentage of the particles in the dataset, the equilibrium between closed and open form in solution is strongly shifted towards the closed form.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the data.

claim: Binding to ARL6GTP acts as a thermodynamic sink that locks the BBSome into the open conformation.
source: Binding to ARL6GTP would thus act as a thermodynamic sink that locks the BBSome into the open conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Small GTPases of the ARF/ARL family undergo conformational changes in three regions upon nucleotide exchange from GDP to GTP: the Switch 1 and 2 regions and the Interswitch toggle.
source: Small GTPases of the ARF/ARL family undergo conformational changes in three regions upon nucleotide exchange from GDP to GTP: the Switch 1 and 2 regions and the Interswitch toggle (Sztul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: BBS1βprop makes contacts with the Switch 2 region and with helix α3 of ARL6GTP.
source: As previously found in the crystal structure of the BBS1βprop–ARL6GTP complex (Mourão et al., 2014), the BBS1βprop makes contacts with the Switch 2 region and with helix α3 of ARL6GTP while the Switch 1 region of ARL6 is readily available for interacting with other, yet unidentified, complexes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation consistent with a previous crystal structure.

claim: The Switch 1 region of ARL6 is readily available for interacting with other, yet unidentified, complexes.
source: As previously found in the crystal structure of the BBS1βprop–ARL6GTP complex (Mourão et al., 2014), the BBS1βprop makes contacts with the Switch 2 region and with helix α3 of ARL6GTP while the Switch 1 region of ARL6 is readily available for interacting with other, yet unidentified, complexes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The 'backside' of ARL6GTP interacts with a loop that connects BBS7βprop and BBS7cc.
source: Interestingly, the 'backside' of ARL6GTP (i.e., the surface on the opposite side of the Switch regions) interacts with a loop that connects BBS7βprop and BBS7cc.
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation.

claim: ARL6 binding to the BBS7βprop-BBS7cc loop will not be gated by the nucleotide state.
source: Given the absence of conformational changes in the backside of ARL6 upon nucleotide exchange, ARL6 binding to the BBS7βprop-BBS7cc loop will not be gated by the nucleotide state, similar to the proposed binding of ARF1 to the γ subunit of the clathrin adaptor AP-1 (Ren et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on structural observations and comparison to another system.

claim: BBS7 was the only subunit unambiguously captured by SMOCtail in in vitro-translated BBSome subunit assays.
source: Using in vitro-translated (IVT) BBSome subunits, we found that BBS7 was the only subunit unambiguously captured by SMOCtail (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: BBS7 was the sole subunit to recognize SSTR3i3.
source: BBS7 was also the sole subunit to recognize SSTR3i3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: The first 19 amino acids of SMOCtail are necessary and sufficient for binding to BBS7.
source: Truncations of SMOCtail revealed that the first 19 amino acids of SMOCtail are necessary and sufficient for binding to BBS7 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from truncation assays with reference to a figure.

claim: The specificity of BBS7 binding to SMO was retained when BBSome subunits were assayed against the first 19 amino acids of SMOCtail.
source: The specificity of BBS7 binding to SMO was retained when BBSome subunits were assayed against the first 19 amino acids of SMOCtail (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: Systematic yeast two-hybrid testing identified a direct interaction between SMOCtail and a BBS7 fragment C-terminal to the β-propeller (BBS7[326-672]; BBS7C).
source: Systematic yeast two-hybrid (YTH) testing using a collection of well-validated constructs (Woodsmith et al., 2017) identified a direct interaction between SMOCtail and a BBS7 fragment C-terminal to the β-propeller (BBS7[326-672]; BBS7C) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as a result from yeast two-hybrid assays with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Deletion of the first 10 amino acids from SMOCtail abolished the YTH interaction with BBS7C.
source: Again, deletion of the first 10 amino acids from SMOCtail abolished the YTH interaction with BBS7C (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a result from yeast two-hybrid assays with reference to a figure.

claim: BBS7 is one of only two BBSome subunits associating with SMOCtail in co-IP studies.
source: In close agreement with our findings, BBS7 is one of only two BBSome subunits associating with SMOCtail in co-IP studies and deletion of the first 10 amino acids of SMOCtail abolishes the interaction with BBS7 (Seo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as agreement with a previous study with a citation.

claim: Deletion of the first 10 amino acids of SMOCtail abolishes the interaction with BBS7 in co-IP studies.
source: In close agreement with our findings, BBS7 is one of only two BBSome subunits associating with SMOCtail in co-IP studies and deletion of the first 10 amino acids of SMOCtail abolishes the interaction with BBS7 (Seo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as agreement with a previous study with a citation.

claim: The first 10 amino acids from SMOCtail and BBS7 are the major determinants of the SMO–BBSome interaction.
source: The congruence of co-IP, YTH and GST/IVT-capture assays strongly supports the conclusion that the first 10 amino acids from SMOCtail and BBS7 are the major determinants of the SMO–BBSome interaction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The first 10 amino acids of SMOCtail form a membrane-parallel amphipathic helix termed helix 8 (H8) in crystal structures of SMO.
source: The location of the BBSome-binding determinant on SMO is surprising because the crystal structures of SMO have revealed that the first 10 amino acids of SMOCtail form a membrane-parallel amphipathic helix termed helix 8 (H8) (Byrne et al., 2016; Deshpande et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013; Weierstall et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from multiple crystal structures with citations.

claim: Mutation of both Trp549 and Trp553 from SMOH8 completely abolished binding to BBS7.
source: Mutation of both Trp549 and Trp553 from SMOH8 completely abolished binding to BBS7, with Trp549 being the major determinant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from mutagenesis assays with reference to a figure.

claim: Trp549 is the major determinant for BBS7 binding in SMOH8.
source: Mutation of both Trp549 and Trp553 from SMOH8 completely abolished binding to BBS7, with Trp549 being the major determinant (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from mutagenesis assays with reference to a figure.

claim: Mutation of Arg550 greatly diminished binding to BBS7.
source: Similarly, mutation of Arg550 greatly diminished binding to BBS7.
evidence: This is stated as a result from mutagenesis assays.

claim: Each residue within the 549WR550 motif contributes to BBSome binding.
source: We conclude that each residue within the 549WR550 motif contributes to BBSome binding.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from mutagenesis data.

claim: All crystal structures of SMO find Trp549 and Trp553 embedded within the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer.
source: The direct binding of BBS7 to Trp549 of SMO was unexpected, because all crystal structures of SMO find these residues embedded within the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from crystal structures with reference to figures.

claim: SMOH8 must be extracted from the membrane for the BBSome to recognize SMO.
source: It follows that SMOH8 must be extracted from the membrane for the BBSome to recognize SMO.
evidence: This is stated as a logical conclusion from the structural and binding data.

claim: 23 of 26 known ciliary GPCRs contain a BBSome-binding motif ([W/F/Y]R) within helix 8.
source: Sequence analysis finds a BBSome-binding motif ([W/F/Y]R) within helix 8 in 20 of the 26 GPCRs known to localize to cilia. Sequences are listed in Supplementary file 3.
evidence: This is stated as a result from sequence analysis with reference to a figure and supplementary file. Note: The text says '20 of the 26' in the figure caption but the claim is based on the figure.

claim: Amphipathic helices generally fold upon insertion into the membrane and remain as random coil in solution.
source: Amphipathic helices generally fold upon insertion into the membrane and remain as random coil in solution (Drin and Antonny, 2010; Seelig, 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Helix 8 is a near-universal feature of GPCRs.
source: Helix 8 is a near-universal feature of GPCRs (Piscitelli et al., 2015) and a peptide corresponding to helix 8 of rhodopsin adopts a helical conformation when bound to membranes but is a random coil in solution (Krishna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: A peptide corresponding to helix 8 of rhodopsin adopts a helical conformation when bound to membranes but is a random coil in solution.
source: Helix 8 is a near-universal feature of GPCRs (Piscitelli et al., 2015) and a peptide corresponding to helix 8 of rhodopsin adopts a helical conformation when bound to membranes but is a random coil in solution (Krishna et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: Membrane requirements for folding of helix 8 are likely generalizable to other GPCRs.
source: Such membrane requirements for folding of helix 8 are likely generalizable to other GPCRs (Sato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a generalization with a citation.

claim: SMOH8 exists in an equilibrium between a folded membrane-embedded and an unfolded state.
source: We therefore propose that SMOH8 exists in an equilibrium between a folded membrane-embedded and an unfolded state, and that it is the out-of-the-membrane, unfolded state that binds to the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the evidence.

claim: It is the out-of-the-membrane, unfolded state of SMOH8 that binds to the BBSome.
source: We therefore propose that SMOH8 exists in an equilibrium between a folded membrane-embedded and an unfolded state, and that it is the out-of-the-membrane, unfolded state that binds to the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the evidence.

claim: BBS7βprop was necessary and sufficient for the interaction with SMOH8 in GST/IVT-capture assays.
source: Further mapping of the SMOH8–BBS7 interaction by GST/IVT-capture assays indicated that BBS7βprop was necessary and sufficient for the interaction with SMOH8 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: Deletion of BBS7cc specifically abolished the SMOCtail–BBS7C interaction in YTH assays.
source: In YTH, deletion of BBS7cc specifically abolished the SMOCtail–BBS7C interaction (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated as a result from yeast two-hybrid assays with reference to a figure.

claim: An extended SMOH8 is recognized by a surface encompassing BBS7cc and BBS7βprop.
source: Thus, while YTH and GST/IVT-capture assays identified different regions of BBS7 recognizing SMOCtail, the regions identified by YTH (BBS7cc) and GST/IVT capture (BBS7βprop) are adjacent to one another in the BBSome structure. To unify these findings, we propose that an extended SMOH8 is recognized by a surface encompassing BBS7cc and BBS7βprop.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal to unify different experimental findings.

claim: BBS7βprop must be within 6 amino acids or ~21 Å of the membrane considering that Trp549 of SMO is contacted by BBS7βprop.
source: Considering that Trp549 of SMO is contacted by BBS7βprop and that the first amino acid of SMO after the 7th transmembrane helix is Lys543, BBS7βprop must be within 6 amino acids or ~21 Å of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a geometric constraint based on the binding data.

claim: BBS7cc must be located within 10 amino acids of the membrane.
source: Similarly, BBS7cc must be located within 10 amino acids of the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a geometric constraint.

claim: SMOH8 must be unfolded to be recognized by the BBSome.
source: We note that if SMOH8 were to remain helical once extracted from the membrane, BBS7βprop would need to be within 9 Å of the membrane. Because no BBSome–ARL6 orientation can be achieved that brings BBS7βprop within less than 15 Å of the membrane, we conclude that SMOH8 must be unfolded to be recognized by the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on geometric constraints.

claim: ARF family GTPases bind lipid bilayers through their amphipathic N-terminal helix inserted in a membrane-parallel orientation within the lipid-headgroup layer.
source: Secondly, ARL6GTP anchors the BBSome to the membrane. Because ARF family GTPases bind lipid bilayers through their amphipathic N-terminal helix inserted in a membrane-parallel orientation within the lipid-headgroup layer, the starting point of the core GTPase domain of ARL6 at Ser15 informs the anchoring of the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex on membranes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ARF family GTPases.

claim: The orientation with respect to the membrane of ARL6GTP in complex with the BBSome is similar to that of other Arf-like GTPases in complex with coat adaptor complexes.
source: In the resulting conceptual model of the membrane-associated BBSome–ARL6GTP complex bound to SMO (Figure 5C), the orientation with respect to the membrane of ARL6GTP in complex with the BBSome is similar to that of other Arf-like GTPases in complex with coat adaptor complexes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; Cherfils, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model with reference to figures and a citation.

claim: The BBSome–ARL6GTP complex displays a convex membrane-facing surface that espouses the contour of the ciliary membrane modeled as a 250 nm cylinder.
source: The BBSome–ARL6GTP complex displays a convex membrane-facing surface, defined by the N terminus of ARL6GTP and parts of BBS2pf, BBS7βprop and BBS9βprop, that espouses the contour of the ciliary membrane modeled as a 250 nm cylinder (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model with reference to a figure.

claim: A convex membrane-binding surface in the GolginGRIP–ARL1GTP or MKLP1–ARF6GTP complexes allows these complexes to associate with concave surfaces.
source: A convex membrane-binding surface in the GolginGRIP–ARL1GTP or MKLP1–ARF6GTP complexes similarly allows these complexes to associate with concave surfaces (Makyio et al., 2012; Panic et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to other systems with citations.

claim: A hydrophobic cluster traced through the surfaces of BBS7cc and BBS7βprop is a strong candidate for sheltering the critical Trp residues in SMOH8.
source: Importantly, a hydrophobic cluster traced through the surfaces of BBS7cc and BBS7βprop reveal a strong candidate for sheltering the critical Trp residues in SMOH8 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the structure with reference to a figure.

claim: The BBSome recognizes lipid headgroups, in particular the phosphoinositide PI(3,4)P2, in liposome-recruitment assays.
source: Liposome-recruitment assays with pure BBSome and ARL6GTP have shown that the BBSome recognizes lipid headgroups, in particular the phosphoinositide PI(3,4)P2 (Jin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: BBS5PH1 contains a perfect match to the PIP-binding motif (K41xxxxxR47xR49).
source: The canonical PIP-binding motif Kxn[K/R]xR is present in the β1-β2 loop of nearly all PH domains that bind PIPs (Isakoff et al., 1998; Vonkova et al., 2015). BBS5PH1 contains a perfect match to the PIP-binding motif (K41xxxxxR47xR49) but no such motif is found in BBS5PH2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: No PIP-binding motif is found in BBS5PH2.
source: The canonical PIP-binding motif Kxn[K/R]xR is present in the β1-β2 loop of nearly all PH domains that bind PIPs (Isakoff et al., 1998; Vonkova et al., 2015). BBS5PH1 contains a perfect match to the PIP-binding motif (K41xxxxxR47xR49) but no such motif is found in BBS5PH2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from sequence analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: Lipid binding to BBS5PH2 is blocked by the edge of a blade from BBS9βprop.
source: Consistent with the absence of a PIP-binding motif in BBS5PH2, lipid binding is blocked by the edge of a blade from BBS9βprop (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The canonical lipid-binding site of BBS5PH1 was occluded by a loop connecting BBS7βprop to BBS9cc.
source: When the canonical PIP-binding site was mapped to the structure of BBS5PH1, the lipid-binding site was occluded by a loop connecting BBS7βprop to BBS9cc (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The PH domains of BBS5 are unable to recognize PIP through their canonical sites.
source: In summary, the PH domains of BBS5 are unable to recognize PIP through their canonical sites.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Lipid binding to the predicted atypical site of BBS5PH1 extensively clashes with BBS8TPR8-9.
source: More recently, the crystal structure of the PH domain of ASAP1 has provided singular evidence for an atypical PIP-binding (A) site (Jian et al., 2015). In BBS5PH1, lipid binding to the predicted A site extensively clashes with BBS8TPR8-9 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Lipid binding to the putative atypical site of BBS5PH2 would cause no steric clash.
source: In BBS5PH2, lipid binding to the putative A site would cause no steric clash (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: It is very unlikely that the atypical site of BBS5PH2 participates in lipid binding of the BBSome.
source: However, considering that the distance between the membrane and the A site of BBS5PH2 exceeds 1 nm and considering the limited evidence for the existence of A sites in PH domains, it is very unlikely that the A site of BBS5PH2 participates in lipid binding of the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on geometric and literature considerations.

claim: The surface of the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome exhibited considerably fewer negative charges facing the membrane than the surface of BBSome alone.
source: Interestingly, the surface of the ARL6GTP-bound BBSome exhibited considerably fewer negative charges facing the membrane than the surface of BBSome alone (compare Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from electrostatic surface analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The surfaces closest to the membrane are generally positively charged in the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex structure.
source: While some negatively charged surfaces facing the membrane remained, the surfaces closest to the membrane are generally positively charged in the BBSome–ARL6GTP complex structure.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from electrostatic surface analysis.

claim: IFT38/CLUAP1 is the only IFT-B subunit to consistently interact with the BBSome in systematic affinity purification studies.
source: We next considered binding of the BBSome to IFT. IFT38/CLUAP1 is the only IFT-B subunit to consistently interact with the BBSome in systematic affinity purification studies (Boldt et al., 2016) and a recent study found that the C terminus of IFT38 interacts with the BBSome in visual immunoprecipitation (VIP) assays (Nozaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The C terminus of IFT38 interacts with the BBSome in visual immunoprecipitation (VIP) assays.
source: We next considered binding of the BBSome to IFT. IFT38/CLUAP1 is the only IFT-B subunit to consistently interact with the BBSome in systematic affinity purification studies (Boldt et al., 2016) and a recent study found that the C terminus of IFT38 interacts with the BBSome in visual immunoprecipitation (VIP) assays (Nozaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding with a citation.

claim: IFT38 directly interacts with the BBSome in GST-capture assays with pure BBSome.
source: Using GST-capture assays with pure BBSome, we confirmed that IFT38 directly interacts with the BBSome and that the C-terminal domain of IFT38 is necessary and sufficient for this interaction (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: The C-terminal domain of IFT38 is necessary and sufficient for interaction with the BBSome.
source: Using GST-capture assays with pure BBSome, we confirmed that IFT38 directly interacts with the BBSome and that the C-terminal domain of IFT38 is necessary and sufficient for this interaction (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated as a result from binding assays with reference to a figure.

claim: The C-terminal tail of IFT38 (aa 329–413) is predicted to be unstructured and is extremely acidic with 30 Glu or Asp in its 85 amino acids, giving it a theoretical pI of 4.03.
source: The C-terminal tail of IFT38 (aa 329–413) is predicted to be unstructured and is extremely acidic with 30 Glu or Asp in its 85 amino acids, giving it a theoretical pI of 4.03 (Figure 7B).

claim: VIP assays identified BBS9 as the major binding subunit of IFT38C, with contributions from BBS2 and BBS1.
source: As VIP assays identified BBS9 as the major binding subunit of IFT38C, with contributions from BBS2 and BBS1, we reasoned that a BBS9 domain in close proximity to BBS2 and BBS1 should be responsible for IFT38C binding.
evidence: This is stated as a result from VIP assays.

claim: An extended positive patch is found in BBS9GAE.
source: The C terminus of BBS9 (GAE, pf, hp, CtH) sits atop BBS1GAE and connects to BBS2hp and an extended positive patch is found in BBS9GAE (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated as a structural observation with reference to a figure.

claim: The positive patch in BBS9GAE is a strong candidate for the IFT38C interaction.
source: This positive patch is therefore a strong candidate for the IFT38C interaction and its orientation away from the membrane makes it well-positioned to interact with IFT trains associated with the axoneme.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on structural and biochemical data.

claim: The candidate IFT38C-binding region is oriented away from the membrane and well-positioned to interact with IFT trains associated with the axoneme.
source: This positive patch is therefore a strong candidate for the IFT38C interaction and its orientation away from the membrane makes it well-positioned to interact with IFT trains associated with the axoneme.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: The candidate IFT38-binding region does not undergo any measurable change upon conformational opening of the BBSome.
source: First, IFT38 interacts with the BBSome in systematic immuno-precipitation/mass spectrometry studies, in VIP assays, and in GST capture of pure BBSome. The candidate interacting region is diametrically opposite from the ARL6-binding region and does not undergo any measurable change upon conformational opening.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from structural comparison.

claim: BBS7βprop and BBS7cc appear equally accessible in the closed and open conformation.
source: Second, BBS7βprop and BBS7cc appear equally accessible in the closed and open conformation (Figures 1A and 2A and Video 1), suggesting that the conformational change is unlikely to directly increase the affinity of BBSome for its cargo SMO.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from structural comparison with reference to figures and a video.

claim: The conformational change is unlikely to directly increase the affinity of BBSome for its cargo SMO.
source: Second, BBS7βprop and BBS7cc appear equally accessible in the closed and open conformation (Figures 1A and 2A and Video 1), suggesting that the conformational change is unlikely to directly increase the affinity of BBSome for its cargo SMO.

claim: The densities for BBS7βprop and BBS7cc are much better defined in the ARL6GTP-bound structure.
source: It should nonetheless be noted that the densities for BBS7βprop and BBS7cc are much better defined in the ARL6GTP-bound structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), thus suggesting that these regions become less mobile upon ARL6GTP binding.

claim: BBS7βprop and BBS7cc become less mobile upon ARL6GTP binding.

source: This change in mobility of BBS7βprop and BBS7cc are consistent with the direct binding of the backside of ARL6 to the BBS7βprop-BBS7cc connector loop.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: ARL6GTP binding to the BBSome may lock the cargo-binding determinants of the BBSome in an orientation that is optimal for cargo binding.
source: ARL6GTP binding to the BBSome may thus lock the cargo-binding determinants of the BBSome in an orientation that is optimal for cargo binding.

claim: Deletion of the BBSome-binding domain from IFT38 in cells did not grossly alter BBSome distribution in cilia or affect the ability of the BBSome to constitutively remove SMO from cilia.
source: Surprisingly, deletion of the BBSome-binding domain from IFT38 in cells did not grossly alter BBSome distribution in cilia or affect the ability of the BBSome to constitutively remove SMO from cilia, but it did interfere with GPR161 exit (Nozaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: Deletion of the BBSome-binding domain from IFT38 interfered with GPR161 exit.
source: Surprisingly, deletion of the BBSome-binding domain from IFT38 in cells did not grossly alter BBSome distribution in cilia or affect the ability of the BBSome to constitutively remove SMO from cilia, but it did interfere with GPR161 exit (Nozaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study.

claim: IFT38 assists the BBSome with a subset of its duties rather than in cohesion between BBSome and IFT trains.
source: These results suggest that IFT38 assists the BBSome with a subset of its duties rather than in cohesion between BBSome and IFT trains.

claim: The recruitment of BBSome to large retrograde trains depends on ARL6.
source: It thus remains conceivable that the interaction of the BBSome with IFT-B is gated by ARL6GTP. In support of this hypothesis, we found that the recruitment of BBSome to large retrograde trains depends on ARL6 (Ye et al., 2018).

source: All our binding studies consistently identify BBS7 as the BBSome subunit responsible for the binding to SMO H8 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the binding studies with reference to a figure.

source: However, earlier co-IP studies found that the SMO C-tail interacts both with BBS7 and BBS5 (Seo et al., 2011).

evidence: This is stated as an observation from the binding assays with reference to figures.

source: It is thus possible that the cargo binding observed for the core BBSome missing BBS7 is based on interactions mediated by BBS5.

source: Our results show that the BBSome can only interact with SMO if its amphipathic H8 is extracted from the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Aromatic residues in helix 8 of ciliary GPCRs will point towards the core of the membrane.
source: Searching for the BBSome-binding motif [W/F/Y][K/R] (Klink et al., 2017) within H8 of the 26 known ciliary GPCRs revealed that 23 of them contained a BBSome-binding motif in their helix 8 (Figure 4C). Considering that aromatic residues will point towards the core of the membrane in these H8, the broad distribution of BBSome-binding motifs suggests that the BBSome may bind to extracted H8 in nearly all ciliary GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration based on the amphipathic nature of helix 8.

claim: The BBSome may bind to extracted H8 in nearly all ciliary GPCRs.
source: Considering that aromatic residues will point towards the core of the membrane in these H8, the broad distribution of BBSome-binding motifs suggests that the BBSome may bind to extracted H8 in nearly all ciliary GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on sequence analysis.

claim: It will be a rare event for H8 to leave the membrane and be available for capture by the BBSome.
source: Because of its amphipathic nature, it will be a rare event for H8 to leave the membrane and be available for capture by the BBSome.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the amphipathic nature of H8.

claim: The close proximity of the ARL6-binding site ensures that the binding site for the SMO C-tail is close to the membrane and in the best position to bind H8 as soon as it leaves the membrane.
source: It is thus noteworthy that the region of the BBSome involved in SMO C-tail binding is located directly adjacent to its ARL6-binding site (Figure 5C,D). The close proximity of the ARL6-binding site that tethers the BBSome to the membrane will ensure that the binding site for the SMO C-tail is also close to the membrane and will thus be in the best position to bind H8 as soon as it leaves the membrane.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the structural arrangement.

claim: Helix 8 in class A GPCRs are frequently palmitoylated near their C termini.
source: SMOH8 is predicted to be capped by a palmitoylated cysteine (Cys554), similar to helix 8 in class A GPCRs, which are frequently palmitoylated near their C termini (Piscitelli et al., 2015).

source: Our structures reveal that binding of ARL6GTP results in the formation of a cleft in the BBSome that is close to BBS7βprop and BBS7cc (Figure 5D), the region involved in SMOH8 binding, and is thus a potential location for the predicted cavity needed to shelter the SMO C-tail.
